A calk is a small, sharp, pointed metal projection — essentially a spike or a cleat — that is fixed onto the bottom of a horseshoe or the heel and sole of a work boot. Its entire purpose is grip: to dig into slippery ground (like ice, hard-packed snow, or wet pavement) so that the horse or the person wearing the boots doesn't slip and fall.

Think of it the way you'd think about cleats on a football boot, or crampons on a mountaineer's boot — just older, simpler, and made of iron or steel.
What it looks like and where it sits

On a horseshoe, calks are small downward-pointing metal bumps or spurs forged or welded onto the shoe itself — usually at the toe and at the heels of the shoe. When the horse steps down, these tiny projections pierce or grip the ground surface, giving the hoof traction that a flat, smooth shoe simply cannot provide.

On a boot, calks are metal pieces (sometimes spikes, sometimes heel caps with sharp edges) attached to the sole or heel to stop the wearer from skidding. Loggers and workers doing outdoor labor on slippery terrain historically wore boots fitted with calks for exactly this reason. In fact, in logging culture, boots with calks are so iconic that they're often simply called calk boots or caulk boots (the two spellings are used interchangeably).
Why it matters: the problem it solves

A flat horseshoe on icy cobblestones or a frozen road is genuinely dangerous — a horse can slip, fall, and injure itself or its rider. Similarly, a worker on an icy slope or a wet log deck can fall badly. The calk solves this by converting the flat, sliding surface of the shoe or boot into something that actively bites into the ground.

This is why calks were (and still are) especially important in:

  • Cold climates, where horses had to work on frozen or icy roads
  • Mountainous or uneven terrain, where footing is unpredictable
  • Logging, where workers walked across floating logs or steep, muddy hillsides

This is worth clearing up because the two words look almost identical and you will encounter both.

Caulk (the far more common word today) refers to the soft, paste-like material — often white or clear — that you squeeze from a tube to seal gaps between surfaces, like where a bathtub meets a tiled wall, or around a window frame to keep out drafts and water. It's a sealant.

Calk (this word) in its primary noun sense refers to the metal spike or projection described above. It is a grip device, not a sealant.

The confusion arises because "calk" is also an older or variant spelling of "caulk" — historically, workers would "calk" a ship's hull meaning they'd seal its gaps with fibrous material and tar. But when you see "calk" used specifically as a noun referring to a thing (not an action), the meaning is almost always the metal spike on a horseshoe or boot, not the sealant.
Quick mental picture to lock it in

Imagine a horse trying to walk across an icy road. Its smooth iron shoes skate across the surface and it struggles to stay upright. Now a blacksmith adds small, downward-pointing iron spikes to the underside of those shoes. The horse can now walk with confidence — each step, those spikes grip the ice. Those spikes are calks.

A calk (noun) is a pointed metal spike or projection attached to the underside of a horseshoe or work boot, designed to provide traction and prevent slipping on ice, hard ground, or other slippery surfaces. It is essentially the pre-industrial equivalent of a cleat or crampon — a simple but effective grip device. The word is sometimes spelled the same as "caulk," but as a noun referring to a physical object, it almost always means this spike, not the sealant paste.
